title: The ENTIRE History of Inflation in 16 Minutes

p.head: England, then the UK · Bank of England and ONS

beats.text: In the next 16 minutes you will see why prices crept up for 700 years, then rose 111 times, and what broke.
beats.visual: 817 years of English and UK prices, log scale, drawing left to right; tags 'x15' and 'x111' appear on the line

title: The entire history
of inflation
p.sub: from Roman silver to the price shock of 2022

chart.head: England, then the UK · Bank of England and ONS

beats.text: This is the entire history of inflation, from Roman silver coins to the price shock of 2022. The line on screen is the Bank of England's own record of English prices, going back to the year 1209. For seven centuries it barely climbs. Then it takes off.

p.head: English prices: how many times they multiplied · Bank of England, ONS
p.foot: annual averages; BoE millennium dataset to 2015, ONS CPI after

beats.text: Here is the scale of it. In the 704 years from 1209 to 1913, prices in England rose about fifteen times. In the 112 years since 1913, they have risen a hundred and eleven times.

p.head: Five patterns, from Rome to 2022

beats.text: So why was money so steady for so long, and why did that end? By the end of this video you will see the five patterns that turn up again and again, from Rome to 2022.
beats.visual: five numbered slots, blank, filled in chapter 9

p.head: In this video
items: Rome: less silver in every coin
The silver flood
Paper money
The long calm
War, and Weimar
The record breakers
The Great Inflation
The surge of 2021 to 2023
The patterns

beats.text: We go in order: Rome, the silver flood, paper money, the long calm, the hyperinflations, the 1970s, the surge of 2021 to 2023, and then the patterns.

beats.chapter: 1 · Rome: less silver in every coin

lines: Each unit of money buys less.

beats.text: First, a definition. Inflation is a rise in prices in general: each unit of money buys less. For most of history, money was metal, so the simplest way for a government to make more money was to put less metal in each coin.

beats.chapter: 1 · Rome: less silver in every coin

p.head: Rome's silver coin under Augustus

beats.text: Rome's silver coin, the denarius, first appeared around 211 BC, during the war with Hannibal. Under Augustus, the first emperor, it was essentially pure silver, one eighty-fourth of a Roman pound: about 3.9 grams.
beats.visual: a drawn denarius with its weight and fineness
beats.say: Rome's silver coin, the den-airy-us, first appeared around 211 BC, during the war with Hannibal. Under Augustus, the first emperor, it was essentially pure silver, one eighty-fourth of a Roman pound: about 3.9 grams.

beats.chapter: 1 · Rome: less silver in every coin

p.head: Nero, AD 64: 1/96 of a pound, and less silver in it

beats.text: In AD 64, Nero made it lighter, one ninety-sixth of a pound, and put less silver in it. How much less is still argued. The traditional figure is a fineness of about 93 percent. A modern laboratory study says it fell to about 80.
beats.visual: two drawn coins with the two fineness figures
beats.say: In A.D. 64, Nero made it lighter, one ninety-sixth of a pound, and put less silver in it. How much less is still argued. The traditional figure is a fineness of about 93 percent. A modern laboratory study says it fell to about 80.

beats.chapter: 1 · Rome: less silver in every coin

p.head: Silver in one antoninianus, grams · RIC

beats.text: In 215, Caracalla launched a new coin, the antoninianus. It was valued at two denarii, but it held only about one and a half denarii's worth of silver. Then it shrank. Over about thirty years in the middle of the third century, its silver fell from roughly 2.2 grams to less than a tenth of a gram. It was almost entirely copper.
beats.say: In 215, Caracalla launched a new coin, the antoninianus. It was valued at two den-airy-eye, but it held only about one and a half den-airy-eye's worth of silver. Then it shrank. Over about thirty years in the middle of the third century, its silver fell from roughly 2.2 grams to less than a tenth of a gram. It was almost entirely copper.

beats.chapter: 1 · Rome: less silver in every coin

p.head: Silver per denarius of face value, grams · our arithmetic on published figures
p.bigSub: less silver for the same money
p.foot: a Roman pound taken as 327–329 g

beats.text: Here is our arithmetic on those published figures. Under Augustus, one denarius of face value carried about 3.9 grams of silver. By the low point, the same face value carried less than 0.05 grams. That is more than 98 percent less silver for the same money. Debasement let the state pay out more coins from the same silver.
beats.say: Here is our arithmetic on those published figures. Under Augustus, one den-airy-us of face value carried about 3.9 grams of silver. By the low point, the same face value carried less than 0.05 grams. That is more than 98 percent less silver for the same money. Debasement let the state pay out more coins from the same silver.

beats.chapter: 1 · Rome: less silver in every coin

p.title: EDICT ON MAXIMUM PRICES
p.foot: drawn as a diagram, not a copy of the inscription

beats.text: In 301, the emperor Diocletian issued the Edict on Maximum Prices. It set a legal top price for goods and wages across the empire, and the penalty for breaking it was death. It proved impossible to enforce across an empire that size.
beats.visual: a stylised tablet drawn in code
beats.say: In 301, the emperor Dye-oh-klee-shun issued the Edict on Maximum Prices. It set a legal top price for goods and wages across the empire, and the penalty for breaking it was death. It proved impossible to enforce across an empire that size.

p.head: Potosí silver, found 1545, to Seville

beats.text: Next, a flood. In 1545, silver was found at Potosí, in what is now Bolivia. It went by ship to Panama, and from there across the Atlantic to Seville.
beats.say: Next, a flood. In 1545, silver was found at Potoh-see, in what is now Bolivia. It went by ship to Panama, and from there across the Atlantic to Seville.

p.head: Silver arriving in Seville, tonnes a year · Hamilton, via Munro

beats.text: The economic historian Earl Hamilton counted the treasure arriving in Seville. From the late 1540s to the early 1590s, yearly silver imports rose about fifteen times, from around 19 tonnes a year to around 274 tonnes.

p.head: Hamilton's index of Spanish prices, in silver

beats.text: Prices followed. Hamilton's index of Spanish prices, measured in silver, rose about three and a half times between the 1510s and the 1640s. Historians call it the price revolution.
beats.visual: bars: Spanish index at the two ends

p.head: England (Bank of England, yearly) and Spain (Hamilton) on the same years

beats.text: We ran the same comparison on the Bank of England's English prices, over the same years. England's rose even more: nearly six times. Part of that is England's own doing. In the 1540s, England debased its own coins, in what is called the Great Debasement.
beats.visual: England and Spain from the same start

p.sub: Spanish prices began rising before much American silver arrived

beats.text: Silver was not the only cause. Spanish prices had started rising before much American silver arrived, and historians still debate how much was silver and how much was a growing population.

p.head: The price revolution, spread over 135 years (1511–15 to 1646–50)

beats.text: Now spread the rise out. Over those 135 years, this revolution ran at under one percent a year in Spain, and about 1.3 percent in England. Today's central banks aim for two. By a modern standard, the price revolution was low inflation. It only looked like a revolution because, for centuries before it, prices had hardly moved at all.

p.head: Sichuan, western China
note: issued by the Song state from 1023

beats.text: The third big change was paper. In Sichuan, in western China, private firms began issuing paper notes called jiaozi in the 990s. In 1023, the Song state took over the issue itself. Paper has one property that matters here: there is no metal to run out of.
beats.visual: map of Sichuan with a note card
beats.say: The third big change was paper. In Sitch-wahn, in western China, private firms began issuing paper notes called jow-dzuh in the 990s. In 1023, the Song state took over the issue itself. Paper has one property that matters here: there is no metal to run out of.

p.head: Yuan China, 1346 to 1355 · Guan, Palma & Wu
foot: stability, then mild inflation, then hyperinflation
money issued to pay for war

beats.text: Under the Mongol Yuan dynasty, Khubilai Khan made paper the only legal tender, and took bronze coins and precious metals out of use. A recent study of Yuan prices found the pattern this video keeps finding: stability, then mild inflation, then hyperinflation, driven by money issued to pay for war. Between 1346 and 1355, prices rose 12.7 percent a year. That is close to tripling in nine years.
beats.say: Under the Mongol Yoo-ahn dynasty, Koo-bee-lie Khan made paper the only legal tender, and took bronze coins and precious metals out of use. A recent study of Yoo-ahn prices found the pattern this video keeps finding: stability, then mild inflation, then hyperinflation, driven by money issued to pay for war. Between 1346 and 1355, prices rose 12.7 percent a year. That is close to tripling in nine years.

beats.text: The next dynasty, the Ming, kept paper money at first. By about 1425, its notes had stopped working as currency.

p.name: John Law
p.foot: an engraved name card, drawn; no portrait

beats.text: Europe tried paper three centuries later. In 1716, a Scotsman called John Law set up the General Bank in Paris. In December 1718 it became the Royal Bank. Law used the bank, and a trading company later known as the Mississippi Company, to restructure France's public debts.
beats.visual: an engraved name card drawn in code; timeline 1716, 1718, 1720

p.head: France, 1720 · Velde, Chicago Fed

beats.text: According to François Velde, an economist at the Chicago Fed, the money in circulation multiplied by 2.6. In January 1720 alone, Paris prices rose 25 percent. At a two percent target, that is eleven years of inflation in one month. By the end of 1720 the system had collapsed, and Law had fled France.
beats.visual: one month of Paris prices vs eleven years at 2%
beats.say: According to Fran-swah Vel-duh, an economist at the Chicago Fed, the money in circulation multiplied by 2.6. In January 1720 alone, Paris prices rose 25 percent. At a two percent target, that is eleven years of inflation in one month. By the end of 1720 the system had collapsed, and Law had fled France.

p.head: The long calm · Bank of England

beats.text: After the price revolution, English prices almost stopped rising. From 1650 to 1913, they went up just 35 percent in total. That is about a tenth of a percent a year, for two and a half centuries.

p.head: Share of years with falling prices, by century · England and UK

beats.text: And prices did not only go up. In the 1700s, prices fell in 46 years out of a hundred. In the 1800s, they fell in exactly half. A falling year was as normal as a rising one.
beats.visual: bars: share of falling years by century

p.head: War with France, 1797 to 1821 · Bank of England

beats.text: The spikes came in wartime. In 1797, at war with France, the Bank of England stopped exchanging its notes for gold. It did not start again until 1821. In the data, prices rose 30 percent in the single year 1800, and by 1813 they were about 70 percent higher than in 1797.

p.head: The 1913 price level was first reached in 1799

beats.text: Then the war ended, gold came back, and prices drifted down again. By 1850 they were below where they had been in 1799. In fact, a shopper in 1913 was paying about what a shopper in 1799 had paid. The price level of 1913 had first been reached more than a century earlier.
beats.visual: a horizontal guide at the 1913 level, touching 1799

p.head: Worst years on the US record, December to December · CPI-U

beats.text: The First World War broke the calm everywhere at once. In America, the price level doubled between 1913 and 1920: seven years. The worst single year on the US record, December to December, is 1918, at 20.4 percent. In Britain, prices rose more than two and a half times between 1913 and 1920.
beats.visual: bars: the five worst US years

p.head: Up in war, down in peace · CPI-U and Bank of England, annual

beats.text: And then, in both countries, prices fell back. In the twelve months to June 1921, US prices fell 15.8 percent. By 1933, American prices were about a third below their 1920 level, and British prices fell by more than a third between 1920 and 1934. The old pattern, up in war and down in peace, still held. Germany was different.

p.head: January 1923: French and Belgian troops occupy the Ruhr

beats.text: Germany's hyperinflation was already under way in 1922. Then, in January 1923, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, in a dispute over unpaid reparations. The German government called on workers there to resist passively, and it paid for that resistance with the printing press.
beats.say: Germany's hyperinflation was already under way in 1922. Then, in January 1923, French and Belgian troops occupied the Roo-er, in a dispute over unpaid reparations. The German government called on workers there to resist passively, and it paid for that resistance with the printing press.

p.head: Germany, October 1923 · Hanke & Krus

beats.text: In October 1923, by the figures of the economists Steve Hanke and Nicholas Krus, German prices rose 29,500 percent in a single month. That is about 21 percent a day. Prices doubled every three point seven days.
beats.say: In October 1923, by the figures of the economists Steve Hank-ee and Nicholas Kroos, German prices rose 29,500 percent in a single month. That is about 21 percent a day. Prices doubled every three point seven days.

p.head: A kilo of bread in Germany, marks (log scale) · Deutsches Historisches Museum
p.foot: November 1923: one US dollar = 4.2 trillion marks (Deutscher Bundestag)

beats.text: The German parliament's own history gives the end point: in November 1923, one US dollar cost 4.2 trillion marks. Germany's history museum gives the price of bread: about 69,000 marks for a kilo in August 1923, and over 200 billion marks in November. That is nearly three million times as much, in three months.
In November 1923 a new currency, the Rentenmark, was issued. One Rentenmark was set equal to one trillion of the old paper marks.
beats.say: In November 1923 a new currency, the Renten-mark, was issued. One Renten-mark was set equal to one trillion of the old paper marks.

p.head: Peak months · Hanke & Krus, World Hyperinflations (2012)
p.foot: their definition of hyperinflation: prices rising at least 50% in a month

beats.text: Germany is the famous case, not the worst. Hanke and Krus count a hyperinflation when prices rise at least 50 percent in a month, and on their list the record belongs to Hungary, just after the Second World War. Hungary's central bank describes a country wrecked by war, under Soviet military occupation, owing reparations, and paying its public spending with new banknotes.
beats.say: Germany is the famous case, not the worst. Hank-ee and Kroos count a hyperinflation when prices rise at least 50 percent in a month, and on their list the record belongs to Hungary, just after the Second World War. Hungary's central bank describes a country wrecked by war, under Soviet military occupation, owing reparations, and paying its public spending with new banknotes.

p.head: Hungary, July 1946 · Hanke & Krus
foot: more than 48 doublings in one month
one peak day = more than 56 years at 2%

beats.text: In July 1946, Hungarian prices rose 41.9 quadrillion percent in one month. That is about 207 percent a day. Prices doubled every fifteen hours. In our own arithmetic on their figure, a price that month doubled more than 48 times. And a single day at the peak was more inflation than 56 years at two percent.

Hungary issued the highest denomination banknote in history: one hundred quintillion pengő, a one followed by twenty zeros. On 1 August 1946 a new currency, the forint, replaced it, at one forint for four hundred octillion pengő. That is a four followed by twenty-nine zeros.
beats.visual: a stylised 100 quintillion pengő note drawn in code; 29 zeros written out
beats.say: Hungary issued the highest denomination banknote in history: one hundred quintillion pen-go, a one followed by twenty zeros. On 1 August 1946 a new currency, the for-int, replaced it, at one for-int for four hundred octillion pen-go. That is a four followed by twenty-nine zeros.

p.head: Zimbabwe
note: spending paid for by creating money

beats.text: Another case is recent: Zimbabwe. By the IMF's count, its economy shrank by about 40 percent between 2000 and 2007. The IMF says the hyperinflation was fuelled by the central bank's quasi-fiscal activities, in plain words, government-style spending paid for by creating money.

p.head: Zimbabwe, 2008
p.foot: estimated from a share price traded in Harare and in London

beats.text: Zimbabwe's statistics office stopped publishing inflation after July 2008, when the annual rate was about 231 million percent. Hanke and Krus estimated the rest from the price of a company's shares traded in both Harare and London. By their figures, the peak came in mid-November 2008: 79.6 billion percent in a month, with prices doubling about every 25 hours.
beats.say: Zimbabwe's statistics office stopped publishing inflation after July 2008, when the annual rate was about 231 million percent. Hank-ee and Kroos estimated the rest from the price of a company's shares traded in both Ha-rah-ray and London. By their figures, the peak came in mid-November 2008: 79.6 billion percent in a month, with prices doubling about every 25 hours.

lines: announced by the central bank, January 2009

beats.text: In January 2009, the central bank announced a 100 trillion dollar note. In early 2009, the government moved to a system that used foreign currencies instead of its own.
beats.visual: a stylised 100 trillion dollar note drawn in code

p.head: Prices stopped falling · CPI-U; Bank of England

beats.text: Within ten years of the Second World War, something quieter but more lasting happened. Prices stopped falling. In the US record, the last time prices were lower one December than the December before was 1954. In Britain's yearly series, the last fall was in 1933, so no one in Britain under ninety has seen prices fall over a full year. Before 1900, almost half of all years did.
beats.visual: US 12-month inflation 1914 to 2026; falls shaded; the dips end in the 1950s

p.head: English and UK prices: each doubling since 1209 · Bank of England, ONS

beats.text: Then came what the Federal Reserve's own history calls the Great Inflation, lasting from 1965 to 1982. Between December 1964 and December 1982, US prices more than tripled. In the 1970s alone they doubled. British prices rose more than three times in the same decade. In our UK series, the fastest doubling in eight hundred years came between 1971 and 1977: six years.

p.head: The Great Inflation · CPI-U

beats.text: Several things piled up. On the evening of 15 August 1971, President Nixon closed the gold window: foreign central banks could no longer swap their dollars for American gold. The same night he froze wages and prices for ninety days. In October 1973, Arab oil producers imposed an embargo, and crude oil prices quadrupled. US inflation reached 12.3 percent at the end of 1974, and 14.8 percent in March 1980.
beats.visual: 1971 gold window and price freeze; 1973 embargo; US 12-month inflation with two peaks

p.head: The Fed's answer · FRED (CPI-U, effective federal funds rate)

beats.text: The end came from the central bank. Paul Volcker became chair of the Federal Reserve in August 1979. That October, the Fed said it would control the growth of bank reserves and let interest rates go wherever that took them. The federal funds rate hit a record 20 percent in late 1980. In the monthly averages, it peaked at 19.1 percent in June 1981.
beats.say: The end came from the central bank. Paul Volker became chair of the Federal Reserve in August 1979. That October, the Fed said it would control the growth of bank reserves and let interest rates go wherever that took them. The federal funds rate hit a record 20 percent in late 1980. In the monthly averages, it peaked at 19.1 percent in June 1981.

p.head: The price: two recessions · FRED (CPI-U, unemployment rate)

beats.text: The price was two recessions. US unemployment reached 10.8 percent in November 1982. But inflation came down, and from 1983 to 2020 the US twelve-month rate never went above 6.3 percent.

p.head: Peak 12-month inflation, 2021 to 2023 · BLS, Eurostat, ONS
p.foot: UK: the ONS estimates it was last this high in 1981

beats.text: Then 2021. Prices across rich countries rose faster than they had in decades. In December 2021, US inflation passed 7 percent for the first time since 1982. It peaked at 9.1 percent in June 2022. In the euro area it reached 10.6 percent in October 2022. In the UK, 11.1 percent the same month, and the Office for National Statistics estimates it was last that high in 1981.

p.head: US prices over three years · CPI-U, December to December

beats.text: Put it in levels. In the three years from December 2020 to December 2023, US prices rose 17.8 percent. In the three years before the pandemic, they had risen 6.4 percent.

p.label: Bank of England explainer · paraphrased
lines: a large impact on energy and food prices
Still argued: how much extra demand added

beats.text: The Bank of England names two shocks: the coronavirus pandemic, then Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which had a large impact on energy and food prices. Economists still argue about how much extra demand, helped by government support during the pandemic, added on top.

Central banks responded as Volcker had, more gently. The Federal Reserve's target range went from near zero in March 2022 to between 5.25 and 5.5 percent by July 2023. Inflation came down. But prices did not. By October 2026, US prices were 29.6 percent above their level in December 2020. A slower rise is not a fall.
beats.visual: fed funds and inflation 2019 to 2026; a second panel shows the price level still climbing
beats.say: Central banks responded as Volker had, more gently. The Federal Reserve's target range went from near zero in March 2022 to between 5.25 and 5.5 percent by July 2023. Inflation came down. But prices did not. By October 2026, US prices were 29.6 percent above their level in December 2020. A slower rise is not a fall.

p.head: Five patterns, from Rome to 2022
items: A government that needs money, usually for war
More money, or fewer goods
Price controls treat the symptom
It ends when people trust the money again
A little inflation, all the time, is new

beats.text: So, the five patterns, from Rome to 2022.

p.head: Worst years since 1900 · US December to December; UK annual · red: world-war and post-war years

beats.text: One. The trigger is usually a government that needs money, and the most common reason is war. Rome paid its way in thinner coin. Britain stopped paying out gold in 1797, at war with France. The Yuan printed for war. In the US record, the four worst years are 1917, 1918, 1919 and 1946. In Britain since 1900, four of the five worst years came in the two world wars.
beats.visual: worst years, US and UK, war years marked
beats.say: One. The trigger is usually a government that needs money, and the most common reason is war. Rome paid its way in thinner coin. Britain stopped paying out gold in 1797, at war with France. The Yoo-ahn printed for war. In the US record, the four worst years are 1917, 1918, 1919 and 1946. In Britain since 1900, four of the five worst years came in the two world wars.

ex: Potosí silver · the presses of 1923 and 1946
Zimbabwe's shrinking economy · the oil embargo

beats.text: Two. Inflation is more money chasing the same goods, or the same money chasing fewer goods, and the worst cases have both. Silver from Potosí was more money. The printing presses of 1923 and 1946 were more money. Zimbabwe's shrinking economy and the oil embargo were fewer goods.
beats.say: Two. Inflation is more money chasing the same goods, or the same money chasing fewer goods, and the worst cases have both. Silver from Potoh-see was more money. The printing presses of 1923 and 1946 were more money. Zimbabwe's shrinking economy and the oil embargo were fewer goods.

beats.text: Three. Price controls treat the symptom. Diocletian's edict could not be enforced. Nixon froze prices in August 1971, when US inflation was 4.6 percent. By December 1979 it was 13.3.
beats.say: Three. Price controls treat the symptom. Dye-oh-klee-shun's edict could not be enforced. Nixon froze prices in August 1971, when US inflation was 4.6 percent. By December 1979 it was 13.3.

p.head: How the worst ones ended
items: A new currency: Germany 1923, Hungary 1946
Someone else's currency: Zimbabwe 2009
Painful interest rates: the US, 1979 to 1982

beats.text: Four. It ends when people trust the money again, and that is never free. Germany and Hungary started new currencies. Zimbabwe gave up its own and used other countries' money. America got there through Volcker, at the cost of two recessions.
beats.say: Four. It ends when people trust the money again, and that is never free. Germany and Hungary started new currencies. Zimbabwe gave up its own and used other countries' money. America got there through Volker, at the cost of two recessions.

p.head: England, then the UK · Bank of England and ONS

tags.text: dotted: 2% a year from 2025, a target, not a forecast
at 2% a year, prices double every 35 years

beats.text: Five. The modern world chose a little inflation, all the time. Before 1900, English prices fell in almost one year out of two. Today, the Federal Reserve and the Bank of England both aim for 2 percent a year. At 2 percent, prices double every 35 years. Whether that is the right goal is a debate for economists. What the history shows is that it is new.
beats.visual: the 817-year chart again, with the 2% path drawn forward as a dotted line, labelled 'target, not forecast'

p.head: Limits
items: The long UK series is a splice of many studies
England first, the whole UK later
Early centuries rest on few prices
1225's +50% is probably a harvest, not money

beats.text: Now the limits. The long English series is a splice of many historical studies, put together by the Bank of England. It covers England first and the whole UK later. The early centuries rest on far fewer prices than a modern index, so some of the wildest single years, like a 50 percent jump in 1225, probably reflect harvests rather than money.

p.head: Limits
items: US CPI-U: urban consumers; October 2025 is missing
Hyperinflation figures vary: one source used
Rome: we measured silver, not the cost of living

beats.text: The US figures are the official urban consumer price index, which is missing one month, October 2025. Hyperinflation figures vary between sources, so we used one source, Hanke and Krus, throughout. And for Rome we have the coins but very few prices, so we measured the silver, not the cost of living.
beats.say: The US figures are the official urban consumer price index, which is missing one month, October 2025. Hyperinflation figures vary between sources, so we used one source, Hank-ee and Kroos, throughout. And for Rome we have the coins but very few prices, so we measured the silver, not the cost of living.

p.head: Three things
items: For most of history, prices rose slowly, and often fell
The big breaks came when governments needed money
Gentle inflation that is almost never reversed is new

beats.text: Three things. For most of recorded history, prices rose slowly, and fell almost as often as they rose. The big breaks came when governments needed money: thinner coins, more paper, and in the worst cases a currency that stopped working at all. And since the twentieth century, gentle inflation that is almost never reversed has become the normal state of money.
One last number from the data. Something that cost a hundred dollars in 1913 would have cost about three thousand four hundred dollars in October 2026.
